segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Do you think that, if you had been allowed to continue doing that second-stage deep AI analysis that you wanted to do on the Capella data, we might have had an answer by now on just what the phenomenon is?

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: Well, 16 years later, there has been no continuing investigation. When the funding was stopped after two years, the people on our team that we had trained in understanding the structure of the data that we were looking for were let go on two weeks' notice. They're gone. I know some of them, I know where they went. I fully respect that team, we had trained them in that kind of investigation. They're gone. So the human intelligence was dispersed 15 years ago. I can't go and get it again. Now, the data, the bunch of bits, has been transferred somewhere.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: I don't have a clearance any more. As far as I know, I have never been debriefed from my clearance, which is very unusual. As you know, I had a clearance on the parapsychology project at SRI. When that project terminated, I sat down for a couple of hours with someone who debriefed me and read me the riot act on not betraying the data even if it became public. So I understand the rules. I was never debriefed from the BAASS project, and my colleagues were not. So it's a very strange process, and the data is somewhere. And again, it's a bucket of bits. The question is that those two levels of sanity checks that I had designed were never applied, so they have something with up to 95% false positives.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: Now, I respect those people, I have a good idea where it went. It's a prestigious organization and those are colleagues, and I respect their professionalism, but they haven't investigated those cases. They don't know the witnesses, they don't know where the thing is wrong. And AI, as good as it is now, cannot resolve something which is 95% false positives. If it was the other way around, if 10% is wrong data, the AI could figure it out — it's getting very good — but not at the level where we are. And that's my frustration, that I think you can feel in my voice. Beyond that, I have no authority to argue one way or the other. I did go to Washington and recorded that part of the situation with people in the intelligence committee of the Senate, because I was asked to do that. I was asked to go there and recall, and that's the extent of my testimony.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: So Jacques, tell me what's going on then, because what that suggests to me is that somebody wanted to sabotage your opportunity to get an answer out of the BAASS project. They didn't want you to reach a conclusion. Are we being played? Is the whole UFO/UAP disclosure process all a bit of a joke? Are we ever really going to get to an answer?

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: Again, Ross, I don't want to go beyond my level of professional authority, if you will. I understand the data. I still have the original data, so I can redo some of that, and that's what I'm doing now — some critical questions that I can answer with my own data. So I'm going to be doing that on a small scale. Fortunately, this computer is wonderful, it does things that were impossible 10 years ago, and I can do most of that on my own.
